input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-633: Biologically Inspired Intelligent Systems. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: There have been significant advances in recent years in the areas of neuroscience, cognitive science and physiology related to how humans process information. In this course students will focus on developing computational models that are biologically inspired to solve complex problems. A research paper and programming project on a relevant topic will be required. A background in biology is not required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

Source excerpts:

[nist-ai-rmf]
The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.

[rit-csci-633]
There have been significant advances in recent years in the areas of neuroscience, cognitive science and physiology related to how humans process information. In this course students will focus on developing computational models that are biologically inspired to solve complex problems. A research paper and programming project on a relevant topic will be required. A background in biology is not required. Prerequisites: (CSCI-603 and CSCI-605 and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better) or ((CSCI-243 or SWEN-262) and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall

[scikit-learn-user-guide]
Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

beats.claim: CSCI-633 focuses on developing computational models that are biologically inspired to solve complex problems, drawing on advances in neuroscience, cognitive science, and physiology
beats.example: Students will explore how artificial neural networks mimic biological neural networks to process information
beats.title: Course Context and Scope
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side diagram comparing biological neurons with artificial neural network layers, highlighting input processing, integration, and output transmission

beats.claim: Students must complete prerequisite courses such as CSCI-603, CSCI-605, and CSCI-661 with grades of B or better, or equivalent combinations
beats.example: A student with CSCI-243 and CSCI-262 can satisfy the prerequisite requirement through the alternative pathway
beats.title: Prerequisites and Course Requirements
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart mapping the three prerequisite pathways to the CSCI-633 course entry point, using color-coded arrows to indicate valid routes

beats.claim: The Govern phase establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk within an organization
beats.example: A company might assign a dedicated AI ethics board to oversee model development and deployment decisions
beats.title: NIST Framework Governance Phase
beats.visualDirection: Create a table listing key governance responsibilities such as policy formulation, role assignment, and accountability tracking

beats.claim: The Map phase documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts before deployment
beats.example: Developers would record how a facial recognition system might affect privacy rights and identify specific user demographics
beats.title: NIST Framework Mapping Phase
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a risk mapping template with fields for context description, intended use cases, affected populations, and potential impact categories

beats.claim: The Measure phase uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks and assess system robustness
beats.example: Researchers might conduct user interviews to gather qualitative feedback while running statistical tests to measure model accuracy and fairness
beats.title: NIST Framework Measurement Phase
beats.visualDirection: Present a split-screen graphic showing qualitative methods like survey responses alongside quantitative metrics such as accuracy charts and bias indicators

beats.claim: The Manage phase prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring after deployment
beats.example: An organization might schedule quarterly model audits and maintain a risk response playbook for emerging vulnerabilities
beats.title: NIST Framework Management Phase
beats.visualDirection: Design a risk prioritization matrix with axes for likelihood and impact, showing how resources are allocated to high-risk items

beats.claim: Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation to ensure rigorous analysis
beats.example: A developer would first clean and normalize data, then split it into training and testing sets before training the model
beats.title: Machine Learning Workflow Structure
beats.visualDirection: Draw a linear pipeline diagram showing each workflow stage as a connected block, with arrows indicating data flow from preparation to evaluation

beats.claim: Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently across training and testing data
beats.example: A pipeline might apply standardization to numerical features and encoding to categorical features before passing data to the classifier
beats.title: Preprocessing and Pipeline Construction
beats.visualDirection: Show a pipeline object structure with nested components, highlighting how preprocessing steps are bundled with the model estimator

beats.claim: Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage, and evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors
beats.example: Using test data to scale features would leak information, so developers must fit scalers exclusively on training samples
beats.title: Evaluation and Leakage Prevention
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a data split diagram with training and testing sets, showing preprocessing fitting on training data only and evaluation metrics displayed on testing data

beats.claim: Valid results require checking for leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions while maintaining separate hyperparameter selection from final test
beats.example: A developer would verify that cross-validation splits prevent data leakage and that hyperparameter tuning uses only validation data
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: List a concise checklist with checkboxes for verifying data isolation, monitoring distribution shifts, checking for overfitting, and confirming hyperparameter separation

learningObjectives: Define the core components of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and explain how each phase addresses AI deployment risks.
Explain how machine-learning workflows prevent data leakage and ensure consistent preprocessing through pipeline construction.
Identify how biologically inspired computational models leverage principles from neuroscience and cognitive science to solve complex problems.
